rv.q: "An effervescent throwback to the years when the musical theater was a reliable non-chemical antidepressant...O’Hara’s soprano ranks among the most beautiful I’ve ever heard on Broadway, and it finds a sterling vehicle...The standout among the supporting cast is unquestionably Styles, delivering a confident — no, make that smashing — Broadway debut.

"The clever navigation of this Golden Age musical through today’s waters of gender politics is one of several plusses in an otherwise uneven production that is still able to score some highs in terrific dancing, Kelli O’Hara’s performance and, oh, those Porter songs...
The sad truth — sad at least for a longtime lover of Porter’s songs — is that for all its pizzazz, Kiss Me, Kate itself feels irretrievably dated.
Yet some essential human chemistry is missing.
O’Hara deserves a thousand kisses along with our eternal worship for gracing us with two and a half glorious hours in this altogether wunderbar production.
This new "Kiss Me, Kate" is a joy.
Terrifically performed and staged as this revival is, the kids are more than likely to now see that there is indeed something quite "wunderbar" about this show.
In this show, in every way, Kelli O’Hara kills it.
This Kiss Me Kate is a show that knows exactly what it wants to be and achieves it with abundant style, wit, and most important of all, joy.
Gone is the shiny schmaltz of the Golden Age musical’s previous productions, Ellis instead grounding the piece, when necessarily, in sincerity and reality.

What’s on stage at Studio 54 works—because how could it not, when you have a company headlined by O’Hara and Chase singing such Porter gems as “Another Op’nin’, Another Show,” “So in Love,” and “Wunderbar”?
The design, like much else in this Kiss Me, Kate, keeps perfectly true to the fashions of Cole Porter having a blast with William Shakespeare.
This Kiss Me, Kate is a real treat.

Whether she’s hitting high notes or swatting her male co-star, Kelli O’Hara — funny and fierce — is reason enough to see “Kiss Me, Kate.”

Director Scott Ellis lets O'Hara and Chase and the rest of the cast win the audience over with the glorious music.

This “Kiss Me, Kate” should make even the grumpiest audience member fall in love with the power of great musical theater -- not just today, but from this moment on.
Kiss Me Kate is just that kinda show; one of the finest old musicals around.
It’s singing and dancing puts us gleefully, giddily back in Broadway’s Golden Age.
As a result, Kiss Me, Kate! has never been sexier and more affecting.
This is a jaunty piece of theatre that aims no higher than your heart and scores a direct hit.
To quote the title tune, this Kate is absolutely bellisimo.
Cole Porter’s 1948 masterpiece of dramatic romance and ribald sass is still “Wunderbar!” over 70 years later.

Having Ms. O’Hara in the part opposite Will Chase, it becomes an absolute knockout.

I kept wondering why the show seemed flat overall despite so many enjoyable sections.
Kiss Me Kateis one of my favorite musicals with a strong score and a timeless story, and though there is much to like here, the second act after “Too Darn Hot” seems to fall apart.

Some key casting mistakes keep this well-appointed production from soaring where it should, but the choreography is a knockout and the musical itself so structurally sound and well-written that it cannot fail to entertain—uneven as it is, but still satisfying.
There are several fun numbers and pleasing bits in this Kiss Me Kate, although not as many as I would have liked.
But in Scott Ellis’s anemically directed production, neither has the staying power or depth to celebrate (or reimagine) the 1949. Tony Award-winning hit.
Worse, in my opinion, is that those coming to it for the first time won’t find much to fall in love with.
